summary: Shows how BGP multicast VPN procedures can, with a few small changes, also distribute multicast routing information that is not tied to any VPN.

eli5.summary: Tools made for private networks are reused to share multicast information in the public one.

questions: how to use bgp-mvpn for global table multicast
what is a protocol boundary router
why is single forwarder selection not used for gtm
subtitle: Reusing the BGP machinery built for multicast VPNs to carry ordinary, non-VPN multicast across a backbone.

tldr.problem: Service providers had BGP procedures to distribute multicast routing information for VPN customers, but nothing that applied them to multicast that is not part of any VPN.
tldr.mechanism: Border routers of the core follow the BGP-MVPN procedures using their global table instead of a VRF, with a few changes: the Route Distinguisher is zero, route targets are used differently, and Single Forwarder Selection is not used.
tldr.outcome: One BGP control plane can govern both VPN and non-VPN multicast. These procedures are not interoperable with the separate Global Table Multicast procedures in RFC 7524.

today: RFC 7716 is a Proposed Standard published in December 2015. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Multicast Without a VPN
sections.content:
RFC 6513 and RFC 6514 let a provider offer multicast to its VPN customers, using BGP to distribute control information among the provider edge routers. RFC 7716 shows how the same BGP-MVPN procedures can, with a small number of changes, distribute multicast routing information that is not specific to any VPN.

That information is kept in a router's global table rather than in a VRF, so the result is called Global Table Multicast (GTM). The RFC avoids the term "Internet multicast" because it suggests the streams are public, while GTM can also carry non-public streams such as content distribution to paid subscribers.

The architecture assumes a core network and non-core attachment networks, with a protocol boundary between them. The core routers at the boundary are Protocol Boundary Routers (PBRs). The routers that attach to them are Attachment Routers (ARs). PBRs do the job that PE routers do for MVPN.
sections.eli5: Imagine a mail system built for private clubs. This paper says the same trucks and sorting rules can also serve the whole town with just a few tweaks.

sections.title: Why Reuse the MVPN Procedures
sections.content:
Using the MVPN procedures for GTM gives a single control plane for VPN and non-VPN multicast. The RFC says most MVPN features carry over automatically, including scaling, aggregation, a choice of tunnel technology, segmented and non-segmented tunnels, wildcards for sets of flows, and support for Any-Source Multicast, Source-Specific Multicast and bidirectional multicast, over IPv4 or IPv6.

The document also reuses the same protocol elements, encodings and formats. GTM BGP Updates use the same SAFI and the same NLRI format as MVPN. Where RFC 6513 and RFC 6514 mention the PE-CE interface, read it as the AR-PBR interface, and read the backbone as the part of the network delimited by the PBRs.

The PBRs and ARs may exchange multicast routing information by PIM, IGMP or even BGP, and may exchange unicast routes by IGP, EBGP or IBGP.
sections.eli5: Instead of inventing a new delivery truck, the plan keeps the same truck, the same boxes and the same labels, and only changes a few small details.

sections.title: Route Distinguishers and Route Targets
sections.content:
MVPN uses BGP routes with SAFI 5 (MCAST-VPN). When a PBR originates such a route for GTM, any Route Distinguisher field in the NLRI MUST be set to zero, which is 64 bits of zero. No VRF can have an RD of zero, so this separates GTM routes from VPN routes.

Route Targets (RTs) work differently too. The kind of RT that identifies the upstream node is required, and its Local Administrator field MUST be set to zero, which implicitly names the global table instead of a VRF. Ordinary import and export RTs are OPTIONAL for GTM.

  • With no import RTs configured, a PBR processes a received MCAST-VPN route in its global table only if the route carries no RTs, or carries an upstream-node-identifying RT naming that PBR.
  • If RTs are configured for the global table, they should be distinct from RTs used for MVPN, unless an extranet is intended.
  • RT Constraint (RFC 4684) MAY be used to limit distribution.
sections.eli5: The address label on a GTM package has a blank club number. That blank tells everyone this one is for the town, not for a club.

sections.title: Choosing the Upstream Router
sections.content:
MVPN finds the Upstream Multicast Hop (UMH), the router toward the source of a flow, by looking up the C-root in a VRF. For GTM the lookup is in the global table and the eligible routes have SAFI 1, 2 or 4 instead of 128 or 129. If the global table has imported SAFI 2 routes, those are used. Otherwise SAFI 1 or 4 routes are used. The Upstream RD is always taken to be zero.

The UMH-eligible routes normally carry a VRF Route Import EC and a Source AS EC. GTM has three ways to find the Upstream PBR:

  • Routes with MVPN ECs (MUST be implemented): the ECs may be attached to SAFI 1, 2 or 4 routes. If the Source AS EC is missing, the source AS is the local AS.
  • ECs on the route to the next hop (OPTIONAL): each PBR originates a route to its own address carrying those ECs. This only works if the next hop is not changed on the way, and it must be provisioned.
  • Non-BGP routes (OPTIONAL): deployment-specific methods, such as reading an OSPF link state database or using a full mesh of TE tunnels.

Single Forwarder Selection from RFC 6513 MUST NOT be used for GTM. A route reflector may pass on just one of two comparable routes to a dual-homed source, so PBRs may not all pick the same one. Unlike VPN routes, GTM routes have no RD to keep the two apart. The RFC also explains that BGP ADD-PATH does not fix this, because only the n best paths are reported.
sections.eli5: To find which road leads back to the sender, GTM looks in the town's main address book. If two senders live at the same address, the clubs' tie-breaking trick no longer works.

sections.title: Tunnels and Auto-Discovery Routes
sections.content:
GTM may use either Inclusive Tunnels, which send a flow to all PBRs, or Selective Tunnels, which may reach only a subset. The RFC warns that there may be many more PBRs for GTM than PEs in a given VPN, so a provider using Inclusive Tunnels should think about scale. If most flows do not need to go to every PBR, using only Selective Tunnels may be better.

A PBR is not required to originate an Intra-AS I-PMSI A-D route if it is not using Inclusive Tunnels for GTM and the C-multicast joins are distributed so that their Next Hop does not change. For Inter-AS I-PMSI, S-PMSI and Leaf A-D routes there are no GTM-specific procedures beyond the RD and RT rules.

Source Active A-D routes need a new way to find their originator, because every GTM route has an RD of 0 and the MVPN method assumes distinct RDs. In GTM, the originator may attach a VRF Route Import EC. If the route carries it, the originator is the PE named in the EC. If not, it is the PE in the Next Hop field, which the distributing speaker MUST NOT change.
sections.eli5: You can send a flyer to every house or only to the houses that asked. Sending to every house is easy but wasteful when the town is big.

sections.title: Optional Source Active Filtering and Joins
sections.content:
If many sources send to an ASM group but few PBRs want it, every PBR may still receive many (S,G) Source Active A-D routes. An OPTIONAL procedure limits this. When a PBR originates a C-multicast Shared Tree Join for (RD=0,*,G), it creates an import RT for its global table whose Global Administrator field holds the group address G, with a Local Administrator of zero. It advertises interest in that RT using RT Constraint, and Source Active A-D routes it originates carry the RT. When the join is withdrawn, the RT constraint route is withdrawn and the RT is removed.

The RFC notes the extra RT Constraint routes add overhead, may not pay off if there are few sources per group, and may increase join latency.

For C-multicast joins, the Upstream PE rules of RFC 6514 still apply, with the Upstream PE read as the Upstream PBR. If the PBR knows beforehand that the next hop of the joins does not change, the second RT, based on the next hop of an I-PMSI A-D route, is not needed and should not be present.
sections.eli5: A club can sign up for just the newsletters it wants, so it does not get buried in mail it never asked for.

sections.title: Not Interoperable with RFC 7524's GTM
sections.content:
RFC 7524 also defines a GTM procedure based on the MVPN BGP procedures. The two are different and are NOT interoperable. They can share a network only if they are not applied to the same multicast flows or the same ASM group addresses.

The RFC lists the main differences. RFC 7524 does not use C-multicast Shared or Source Tree Joins and uses Leaf A-D routes in a new NLRI format instead. This document uses the C-multicast routes with an RD of zero, and Leaf A-D routes in the RFC 6514 format. RFC 7524 also uses two different RD values with different meanings, while here a zero RD only means the route is about GTM.

When both are deployed, the PBRs MUST be provisioned so that, for any given group address, all egress PBRs use the same procedures.
sections.eli5: There are two different ways to deliver to the whole town. Both work, but a package must be sent only one way, or the post office gets confused.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Security is mostly that of the base protocols (RFC 6514, RFC 4601 and RFC 5294). The new concern is that routes, attributes and extended communities designed for VPNs are now used outside VPNs. If they leak out, multicast data flows may be distributed in an unintended or unauthorized way.

In VPNs, import and export RTs make it hard to get a route into an unauthorized VRF. In GTM some of that protection is lost, because imports are not restricted to VRFs and the RT infrastructure is not present for global tables.

The RFC also advises care not to delete or modify the VRF Route Import and Source AS extended communities, which could cause streams to be lost or misrouted. Group addresses in BGP routes are only valid within a certain scope, and distributing them outside it may allow unauthorized access to multicast data.
sections.eli5: Tags made for private clubs must not slip out to the street, or someone could get mail meant for others.
